Ibn Qutayba reports the Persian sang (stone) and gil (clay) analysis; al-Alusi calls the hardened-clay sense common and the Persian loan usual. Al-Baydawi gives hardened clay. Al-Qamus, cited by Bursevi, gives clodlike stones or a Persian-derived term. {"id": "16:4/q05", "question": "How does fa-idhā present the jump from drop to disputant?", "turns_on": "Whether the abrupt expression primarily compresses time, uses the outcome as a designation, signals forgetfulness, or dramatizes a surprising moral reversal.", "positions": [{"id": "16:4/q05/p1", "position": "It presents the eventual adult state suddenly, while the intermediate stages are understood or encompassed by creation.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan says the formative stages are left unstated; Samin reports ellipsis as one account and prefers taking khalaqa to cover creation and nurturing until the two qualities appear. {"id": "16:4/q08", "question": "What is the force of the drop-to-disputant contrast?", "turns_on": "Whether the passage's dominant context is proof and benefaction or the denunciation of unbelievers; some readings deliberately include both.", "positions": [{"id": "16:4/q08/p1", "position": "It displays God's power and favor in raising inert, weak fluid to articulate intellect and effective argument.", "reasons": "Mawardi and Wahidi's semanticists state the power reading; Ibn Atiyya names the two extremes and, in a broad reading, counts reason and speech as gifts. Alusi reports some favor it among unbelievers' offenses and Al-Kashf says it fits 'exalted above their associations'; Alusi himself argues the Ya Sin resurrection context differs. Ibn Ashur specifies defense of partners and rejection of monotheistic callers. Tabatabai prefers rebuke in context. Islahi adds hostility toward God and denial of resurrection tied to 50:3 and 16:27. Elmalili includes association of partners and logical or philosophical opposition. Study Quran's IK, Z and R stress denial of power, blessings and resurrection; IK cites 51:56 for the purpose of service. {"id": "16:4/q09", "question": "What does this transformation prove about God's action?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:4/q09/p1", "position": "Human formation and the rise of intellect require a wise, freely acting creator and show His power, oneness, and ability to restore life.", "reasons": "Razi's conditional argument says homogeneous sperm under necessary natural force would yield a sphere; if heterogeneous, its shifting parts could not reliably place brain, heart and other organs. {"id": "16:4/q13", "question": "How does human creation fit the surrounding argument in al-Nahl?", "turns_on": "Whether the local emphasis is the sequence of proofs and blessings or the warning about human resistance; the notes also allow both functions.", "positions": [{"id": "16:4/q13/p1", "position": "It follows cosmic creation as a second, more familiar proof of God's oneness, wisdom, and power, before the passage turns to other created benefits.", "reasons": "Razi moves from celestial bodies to the human, which he calls the noblest body after the heavens, and reads body and soul as paired signs. {"id": "16:15/q04", "question": "What does it mean that mountains keep the earth from swaying?", "turns_on": "The mechanism assigned to mountains: simple anchoring, boat-like ballast, mass on a sphere, crustal formation, or God's customary use of causes; Rāzī and later critics test the physical assumptions.", "positions": [{"id": "16:15/q04/p1", "position": "Mountains hold the earth steady so its inhabitants can live and travel without shaking or tipping.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAbbās through al-Wāḥidī and many others give the direct sense. Al-Zajjāj and Study Quran compare mountains with pegs at 78:7; Biqāʿī says even slight daily tilting would reverse rivers or spill seas. Ṭabāṭabāʾī specifies disruption of livelihoods, and Islahi calls this maintaining balance. Study Quran adds that this stability ends at the Last Day (73:14; 56:4–6; 101:5)."}, {"id": "16:15/q04/p2", "position": "The earth floated and rocked like a boat on water until the weight of mountains anchored it.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī identifies this as the majority account; Bursevī says the earth was created unstable on water and gives 6,673 mountains excluding hills, likening their support to bones in an animal and citing the boneless soothsayer Saṭīḥ.
